title: {{NAME}} and the Unbreakable Crown of the Thornwood
moral: The people who look the most unbreakable are often the ones who most need someone willing to stand beside them.

pages.content:
The Thornwood was not a forest you entered by accident. Its trees grew in angles that discouraged casual passage, their branches weaving overhead into a canopy so dense that even midday light arrived below as a gentle, filtered green. The path through it appeared only to those the Thornwood considered worthy, which was, by most accounts, extremely few people.

The path appeared for {{NAME}} the moment he stepped up to the tree-line, unspooling ahead of him like an invitation written in soil and old leaves.

He followed it for what felt like an hour, and it led him eventually to a clearing where a young woman in armour the colour of storm-clouds sat with her back against the most ancient tree {{NAME}} had ever seen, her helmet off, her knees drawn up, and an expression on her face she clearly did not know anyone was seeing.

She was a superhero. The armour left no doubt about that, heavy and purposeful, marked with the crest of the High Sentinel. Her name, as the whole world knew it, was Mora.

And beside her, pressed close in the way of a creature who knows when it is needed, was a unicorn, tawny-gold and quiet, her mane the colour of autumn.

Mora heard {{NAME}} arrive and her face rearranged itself so quickly and completely that if he had not seen its other arrangement a second before, he would not have known it had ever been different.

'The path doesn't usually let people through,' she said.

'I know,' said {{NAME}}. 'I wasn't sure it would.'

pages.content:
The unicorn's name was Rue, and Rue had been Mora's companion since before the armour, before the title, before the world had developed an opinion about what Mora could and could not do.

'She found me when I was seven,' Mora said, with the directness of someone who has decided that the path bringing {{NAME}} here was reason enough to speak plainly. 'In a field behind my grandmother's house. She's been here ever since.'

Rue regarded {{NAME}} with steady amber eyes, neither welcoming nor suspicious, precisely the gaze of a creature that takes its time and means it.

'There's a princess,' {{NAME}} said. He had heard this part of the story on the road here, pieces of it in market squares and traveller's stops, enough to assemble something close to the whole. 'Princess Wythe. She's been trapped in the Thornwood's inner keep for three days.'

'By the Thornwood's own ward-magic,' Mora said. 'Which activates against anyone it considers threatening. And I am.' She said it matter-of-factly, without self-pity and without especially enjoying it. 'My power signature is too strong. Every time I approach the keep, the ward interprets it as an attack and reinforces. I have tried four times. The princess is perfectly safe inside. I cannot get to her.'

'But someone weaker could,' {{NAME}} said slowly. 'Someone the ward wouldn't read as a threat.'

Mora looked at him. Then she looked at Rue, who had turned her amber eyes to {{NAME}} with an expression that the tawny gold of her coat made impossible to misread.

'You have a plan,' Mora said. Not a question.

pages.content:
The plan had three parts.

Mora would approach the keep from the north, not to enter, but to hold the ward's attention, draw its reinforcements toward herself the way a fire draws moths.

Rue would carry {{NAME}} through the keep's eastern approach, the ward knowing her and tolerating her, as it had since Mora had first found her here.

And {{NAME}} would go in and bring the princess out.

The approach was not peaceful. Mora's attempt from the north filled the Thornwood with a low resonant sound like a bell struck underground, and the ward-magic flowered across the keep's stones in visible pulses of cold blue light. {{NAME}} felt it as pressure in his chest and back teeth, a frequency that said, very clearly: you are noticed.

But not threatened. Not targeted.

Rue moved through the ward's field with the ease of belonging, and {{NAME}} held on to her autumn mane and breathed steadily and watched the blue ward-light pulse away from them toward the north where Mora stood, magnificent and infuriating, drawing everything toward herself that could be drawn.

The keep's inner door was not locked from the inside. The ward protected it from outside. From inside, it simply opened.

Princess Wythe was seated at the keep's single window, watching Mora's display with an expression compounded of admiration and exasperation in roughly equal parts.

'Took you long enough,' she said. Then: 'You rode in on a unicorn.'

'Yes,' said {{NAME}}.

'Wonderful,' she said, and stood up.

pages.content:
Getting the princess out was the part of the plan nobody had fully thought through, because Princess Wythe had not been idle during three days in the keep.

She had discovered, she explained while moving briskly toward the door, that the ward did not simply trap. It also preserved. Inside the keep, deep in the lower chambers, there were artefacts from the old kingdom that had been kept here by the ward-magic for hundreds of years, and Wythe had spent three days cataloguing them.

'I cannot leave without taking the records,' she said. 'They will be lost if the ward destabilises when we go.'

{{NAME}} looked at the records. They were extensive. They were also heavy.

Rue made a sound, low and decided, and {{NAME}} turned. The unicorn had lowered her head and touched her horn to the stack of records, and they had compacted somehow, folded by some quality of unicorn-magic into a package that could be carried in one arm without apparent weight.

From outside, Mora's power signature was intensifying. The ward-bell sound went up in frequency. She was holding it, but not indefinitely.

'Now,' {{NAME}} said.

They went out through the eastern door at speed, Rue ahead, {{NAME}} and Wythe behind, and the ward rushed back after them like a wave returning to sea. Behind them they heard the keep's door seal shut with a sound of finality.

Mora was waiting in the clearing, helmet back on, leaning against a tree with studied casualness, breathing harder than she wanted anyone to notice.

pages.content:
They walked out of the Thornwood together, all four of them, the path still visible and wide enough for Rue to walk beside the three humans comfortably.

Wythe and Mora walked slightly apart from each other in the way of people who have things to say that need the right moment, and {{NAME}} walked with Rue, who smelled of autumn and something dry and warm, like a room full of old books.

At the Thornwood's edge, where the world resumed its ordinary width and noise, Mora stopped. She was facing the trees, and her back had a quality of stillness that was different from her combat stillness. More personal.

'Nobody has ever,' she started, and stopped.

{{NAME}} waited.

'Nobody has ever gone in alongside me rather than waiting to see what I'd do first,' she said. She didn't turn around. 'Rue knew before I said anything. She went for you before I asked.'

Rue pressed her tawny nose against Mora's gauntlet.

'She has good judgment,' {{NAME}} said.

Mora laughed then, short and real, and turned around.

They made camp at the Thornwood's edge while the twilight gathered, and Wythe unrolled the records and began to explain what she had found, and Mora leaned over her shoulder to look, and Rue lay down in the grass with her head in {{NAME}}'s lap.

He was deeply, warmly asleep before the stars had finished arriving.

And somewhere at the edges of sleep, he heard Rue stir, and then a sound like a door in the Thornwood, opening again, from deeper inside than anyone had ever been.
